questions.explanation: #31 says the old library version does not matter because NU7 changes no transaction formats or signing algorithms and PCZTs convey the branch ID; it adds that a migration PR is already up. The tempting first option misreads that PR as a shipped release. #32 accepts the point.
options: Keystone had already released firmware built on the final NU7 crates, so devices only needed the ordinary update before activation.
NU7 changes no transaction formats or signing algorithms, and PCZTs carry the targeted consensus branch ID, so the existing firmware keeps working.
Hardware wallets are exempt, because they only sign transactions that a software wallet has already prepared for the activation height.
The concern was valid for mainnet, but affected users can sign through another wallet until Keystone ships a firmware fix after NU7.
questions.prompt: The readiness list warned that Keystone's firmware was built on a library version with no NU7. What answer did the thread give to that worry?

questions.explanation: #30 raised the Keystone concern, #31 rebutted it, and #32 conceded it 'doesn't hold'. The Sprout claim in #14 and #17 was accepted by the questioner in #16 but was never disputed, so nobody had anything to concede there.
options: After NU7, Sprout funds effectively cannot be spent and are unlikely to be re-enabled by a later upgrade.
Per-block rewards are lowered under ZIP-218, so total issuance per unit of time stays the same.
Keystone's firmware, built on a library with no NU7, put its ability to send after activation at risk.
Consensus around ZSAs is still being debated, with nothing settled.
questions.prompt: Which claim in the thread was conceded by the person who first raised it?

questions.explanation: In #32 the author says he had read the old library version as a problem, but since PCZTs carry the branch ID it does not hold, and he also missed #2312. The release-based option misreads that PR as a shipped firmware, which #31 does not claim.
options: str4d's point that PCZTs carry the consensus branch ID, so the old library version does not matter, plus a migration PR (#2312) that the list had missed.
A new Keystone firmware release shipping the final NU7 crates, which appeared on the project's releases page before the activation height.
Testnet results showing Keystone devices signing NU7 transactions successfully with the old library version still installed on them.
A statement from the Keystone team that its devices would not be used on mainnet until a complete NU7 firmware upgrade had been done.
questions.prompt: What changed Anirudh-712's mind about the Keystone row on the readiness list?

questions.explanation: #28 says the code was updated to Ironwood and 6.3 and is being delivered for testing, with the consensus being to have it on testnet but not in the NU7 deployment. #11 had answered the same question with 'Debate'. #1 says no new transaction formats appear in NU7.
options: ZSAs are scheduled to activate alongside NU7 on mainnet, with the new transaction format arriving on November 5.
ZSAs were dropped after the sentiment polls, and the existing code is no longer being maintained or tested.
ZSAs remain undecided, and a vote on whether to include them will take place before the mainnet decision.
The ZSA code is up to date and going out for testing; the consensus for the past year is to keep it on testnet but out of NU7.
questions.prompt: Which statement matches what #28 said about ZSAs and NU7?

questions.explanation: #8 answers #7 with the ZIP-218 text about dividing the per-block subsidy by a further factor of 3. The halvings option borrows from #1, where the polls concern the NSM and halvings, not the effect of block spacing on issuance.
options: The sentiment poll results on preserving halvings, which fix how much ZEC is issued each year however fast blocks arrive.
Testnet counts of TAZ issued per day since activation, which matched the issuance rate before the upgrade.
A quote from ZIP-218: the per-block subsidy is divided by an additional factor of 3, so issuance per unit of wall-clock time stays the same.
A statement that exchanges will keep crediting rewards at the old rate, regardless of how quickly the new blocks arrive.
questions.prompt: What did #8 offer to show that 25-second blocks would not raise yearly ZEC issuance?

questions.explanation: #13 asked; #14 said the limits are the exchanges' to set and a change would not seem very necessary. #26 describes its confirmation figures as measurement and arithmetic only and reports a deepest reorg of 1 block in its listener window. The tripling option misreads the 30-versus-10 block arithmetic as advice.
options: Unsettled: #14 leaves it to each exchange and sees little need, while #26 only supplies measurements and arithmetic, with no recommendation.
Settled: the thread agreed exchanges must triple their confirmation counts to keep the same time-based safety as before.
Settled: the thread agreed that confirmation counts are fixed by the protocol, so exchanges cannot change them either way.
Settled: the measurements in #26 showed 25-second blocks reorganize so often that exchanges should wait several times longer.
questions.prompt: Where did the thread leave the question of whether exchanges need more confirmations at 25-second blocks?

questions.explanation: #14 and #17 say Sprout funds will effectively be stuck after NU7, that nothing definitive has been decided, and that any hope lies in some other method. #15 only points to a thread discussing a future redemption mechanism, not an approved one.
options: Holders can keep spending them through a one-time migration window that stays open for a while after November 5.
They cannot be spent normally and are very unlikely to be re-enabled by an upgrade; any recovery would need another method, and nothing is decided.
A Sprout redemption mechanism has been approved and will be built into the next network upgrade that follows NU7.
They are unaffected, because Sprout transactions do not use the v4 format that NU7 disables, so wallets can still spend them.
questions.prompt: What did the thread say about Sprout funds once NU7 disables v4 transactions?

questions.explanation: #26 gives thirty 25 s blocks a measured median of 730 s, roughly the 750 s expected for ten 75 s blocks, with a p99 of 1,187 s against 1,409 s for the old target. It presents this as measurement and arithmetic only, answering #13.
options: Thirty 25 s blocks spanned far less time than ten 75 s blocks, so a count of 30 would be faster but less safe.
Thirty 25 s blocks varied more in total time than ten 75 s blocks, which makes the larger count a less reliable wait.
Thirty 25 s blocks gave the same median time as ten 75 s blocks but a wider spread, with a p99 well above 1,409 s.
Thirty 25 s blocks cover about the same expected time as ten 75 s blocks and varied less: a p99 of 1,187 s against 1,409 s.
questions.prompt: In #26, what did the author report when comparing thirty 25-second blocks with ten 75-second blocks?
